name: Fatima Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. This is confidential. What happens on an ordinary day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and lead a ten-person scheduling and payroll support team inside a large care company. The first hour is missing shifts, then I approve corrections and help site managers explain pay slips to staff. I like fixing a lost shift before payday, because somebody’s food money may depend on it. I hate that we can spend three meetings deciding who owns one error.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you reach the lead role, and how secure is life outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied for an MBA while working here and was promoted after I rebuilt the rota process. I live with my sister, no partner or children, and my pay is about normal for this job. We have roughly four months of expenses saved between us, and there are some other large employers nearby. I try a new tool after a colleague shows it works; I use AI sometimes to draft rota notes, never to approve a pay change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that a tidy draft is useful, but the pay record still needs a named person checking it. Staff shouldn’t have to argue with software to get a missing shift fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel reasonably safe in my role because the rota and payroll mess is still there. My sister’s shop hours vary, though, so four months of savings is helpful rather than a permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep our twice-weekly pay correction review and show one colleague how I check AI rota notes against the live shift log. During the first year I’d continue the 120 monthly transfer to our shared emergency account while my sister’s hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own job and careful about the household. The savings give us room to handle a short change in her shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when a worker says the shift log is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask the site manager for the signed timesheet and call the worker back myself. The computer can point to a mismatch; it cannot decide whose word to trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why continue saving if nothing radical changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister’s hours still swing. A quiet AI story doesn’t make my sister’s shop pay predictable.

say: I’d keep a **person checking** each pay correction.
Workers need a **call back** when a recorded shift is wrong.
think: My own **role feels safe** in a plateau.
My sister’s **variable hours** still make savings useful.
Our **four-month reserve** helps if her shop shifts fall.
do: Keep the **pay review** twice weekly and check rota drafts against the live log.
Transfer **120 monthly** to shared emergency savings while shop hours hold.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and careful about home money.
S0.quote: A quiet AI story doesn’t make my sister’s shop pay predictable.
fieldNote: Her **work routine** continues because missing shifts still need checking.
Four months of **shared savings** buffer the household.
She sees a worker’s **call back** as part of correcting the record.

steps.text: Keep the twice-weekly pay correction review and check rota drafts against shift logs
Transfer 120 monthly to shared emergency savings while her sister’s shop hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the company must test automated scheduling against real pay errors and tell staff which tasks will change. I’d bring the worker representatives into the trial before anyone loses a shift-support post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first drafts and checks are much of our day, so a smaller team is quite possible. I’m a strong manager, but a good system might leave fewer people to manage and put me on the list too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask our worker committee to join a six-week test on copied rota records, with staff checking missed allowances. In the first year I’d learn the tool’s audit screen in a paid company course and ask the committee to negotiate advance notice before any support posts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about both my team and my own pay. Having a test and a committee gives me something to do, but it doesn’t guarantee a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the person who checks allowances now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Nia, our allowance clerk, exactly which records the test covers and invite her to find errors with me. I wouldn’t call the trial harmless when her routine work is the first target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still test it if management rejected the committee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would insist on a written reason and bring the issue back to the worker committee. A payroll trial without the people who correct pay is not ready for live wages.

say: I’d demand a **real pay test** before changing schedules.
I’d bring **worker representatives** into the trial.
I’d insist on **notice** before support posts are cut.
think: Routine **drafting and checks** may shrink our team.
Even a strong manager can lose a post when **headcount falls**.
do: Ask the **worker committee** to join a six-week copied-record trial.
Complete a **paid audit-screen course** and seek advance notice of cuts.
feel: I feel **anxious** despite having a group to work with.
S1.quote: A payroll trial without the people who correct pay is not ready for live wages.
fieldNote: She links tool approval to **pay accuracy** and worker voice.
She names **her own job** among those exposed to fewer staff.
The course is **paid** and teaches an audit screen she could use.

steps.text: Run a six-week copied-rota trial with the worker committee checking missed allowances
Complete the paid company course on the scheduling tool audit screen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell site staff to keep copies of their pay records and ask the company for a real plan for displaced workers. I’d say the worker committee needs to see the timetable, not just a reassuring speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nearly all my managing is thinking, checking and explaining, so 2028 could end my role fast. My sister’s shop work may not face hands-on robots until around 2031, but her hours alone would not cover our flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d make copies of my own contract and a household budget, then ask the worker committee to seek a funded transition agreement. Before 2028 I’d enroll in a care training place if accepted and paid; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d take a care assistant role only if the wage and available shifts cover my half of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed by how little time there is. I have four months saved, yet the thought of both of us living on shop shifts keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work when robots come later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hands-on care still needs people until around 2031 in this picture, and I already know the sites. I know that buys time rather than a lifetime guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the transition agreement need to contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid training hours, a clear notice date and help if our old posts close. I would put my name behind the committee’s request, not just nod in a meeting.

say: I’d ask staff to keep **pay records** and demand a displacement plan.
The **worker committee** should see the company timetable.
think: My sister’s shop wages cannot cover **our flat** alone.
Four months saved cannot carry **two adults** for long without my wage.
do: Ask the **worker committee** to seek paid training and notice terms.
Enroll in **paid care training** if accepted and take a care role after 2028 only at a viable wage.
feel: I feel **alarmed** despite four months of savings.
S2.quote: I have four months saved, yet the thought of both of us living on shop shifts keeps me awake.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking deadline** directly threatens her management work.
She treats hands-on care as a **temporary bridge** until later robots.
Her proposed care move depends on **wage and shifts** covering rent.

steps.text: Join the worker committee request for a funded transition agreement before 2028
Enroll in care training before 2028 if accepted with paid hours
Take a care assistant vacancy after 2028 only if wages and shifts cover half the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives the company time to offer real training and written job guarantees during a transition. The committee should check those promises each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into care before the thinking system reaches my job in 2031, instead of taking the first vacancy in panic. The robots around 2034 might then change care work, so I’d want qualifications that employers actually recognize.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next spring I’d enroll in an evening care certificate only if the company pays the fee and lets me keep my hours. I’d keep my management role while I finish it, then apply for open care supervisor posts before 2031; in the first year after AGI, I’d stay only if the care wage covers rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious but less frightened than with 2028. I can count the course months and compare actual job adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company will not pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won’t use our four-month cushion to fund a course for the company’s future staffing. I’d ask the committee to press for paid places and keep reviewing advertised vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would supervising care staff be safe from AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scheduling and paperwork part would still be exposed in 2031. I’d need enough hands-on care skill to work a shift, and I can’t pretend the 2034 robots are irrelevant.

say: I’d seek **paid training** and written transition promises.
The committee should review those **promises yearly**.
I’d ask for **job guarantees** while people finish training.
think: Five years lets me qualify before **2031 thinking AI**.
Care work changes again when **2034 robots** arrive.
I would still need **hands-on care skill** to work a shift.
do: Enroll in an **evening care certificate** if fees and hours are covered.
Apply for a **care supervisor vacancy** before 2031, subject to a viable wage.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to compare real options.
S3.quote: I won’t use our four-month cushion to fund a course for the company’s future staffing.
fieldNote: She refuses to spend the **household cushion** on employer training.
She requires **paid fees** and protected hours before enrollment.
She recognizes that care supervision also contains **exposed paperwork**.

steps.text: Enroll in an evening care certificate if the company pays fees and protects hours
Apply for open care supervisor posts before 2031 only if wages cover rent
Ask the worker committee to press for funded course places

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the company has a decade to stop making each site fight alone for correct pay. I’d ask for workers to help set the rules and for management to show what it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years might let me build a career in care operations and a stronger cushion before 2036. I still think a company could use the time to delay hard decisions until the last year, which is why workers need a say now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d ask the worker committee to negotiate a yearly report on staffing, errors and savings from scheduling tools. I’d set aside 150 a month if our household bills allow, and apply for an open site operations post with hands-on shifts before 2036; in the first year after AGI, I’d keep that post only while it remains paid and staffed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy, though ten years feels like time I could use. I’d rather build a path in daylight than get a notice at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the yearly report change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could see whether fewer errors actually helped workers or simply reduced posts. A public promise means little unless we can compare pay mistakes and staffing year by year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to site work even without a promotion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the posted wage covers my share of rent and the job includes real shifts with staff. I won’t buy a title that leaves me doing only the same exposed spreadsheets.

say: I’d put **workers** in the rule-setting process.
Management should report **staffing and savings** each year.
A decade leaves time for **worker review** before posts change.
think: A decade could build my **care career** and savings.
Management may still delay the **hard decisions** without worker pressure.
do: Negotiate a **yearly report** through the worker committee.
Save **150 monthly** if bills allow and seek a site role with hands-on shifts.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but able to build a path.
S4.quote: I’d rather build a path in daylight than get a notice at the end of it.
fieldNote: Her long-run plan links **worker oversight** with a possible site move.
She will accept a site role only with **real shifts** and viable pay.
She can build savings now, although **household bills** set the monthly limit.

steps.text: Ask the worker committee to negotiate annual staffing error and savings reports
Transfer 150 monthly to savings when household bills allow
Apply for an open site operations role before 2036 only if paid shifts cover rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my role is mostly checking and the shared flat cannot run on my sister’s shop shifts alone. Paid care training, clear notice and a worker agreement on what happens to displaced staff would help. I need an offer with wages, not just encouragement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn’t ask what happens to the care worker whose missing shift is hidden in a system. An unpaid shift is still an unpaid shift, whether a person or a machine loses it.

headlineQuote: An unpaid shift is still an unpaid shift, whether a person or a machine loses it.
portrait: **Fatima**, 27, leads payroll scheduling support after completing an MBA.
Her typical pay and **four-month cushion** help, but her sister’s shop hours vary.
She asks for **worker oversight** before scheduling tools change pay or staffing.
She explores **paid care training** on terms that protect wages and rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her thinking-heavy management role before she can move into paid care work.
whatWouldHelp: A **worker agreement**, paid care training and clear notice would let her choose a viable post.
